docs.title: FRC 829 Programming
docs.text:
The programming side of robotics for FRC Team 829. This site holds the notes, the setup instructions, and the reference material. It is not the robot code itself — that lives in the team's repositories.

The plan for the fall is straightforward:

  1. Java bootcamp. Everyone does this, no exceptions and no prerequisites. You cannot write robot code you cannot debug, and you cannot debug code in a language you are still guessing at.
  2. Then the toolchain. The lab computers are set up for you. You do not need to install anything, and you do not need to open VS Code at all, until the bootcamp is behind you.
  3. Then DigiLib, the team's own library, and start contributing to it.

We are on WPILib 2026.2.1

Everything here targets 2026.2.1 and the roboRIO so that what you learn runs on hardware we already have. The move to 2027 and SystemCore happens in December or after kickoff, once it settles into its final shape — and there is a real amount that changes. We will do it together.

docs.title: Meetings
docs.text:
We meet Mondays, 3:00–5:00 pm in the lab, starting the first Monday after Labor Day and running until kickoff in January.

Two Mondays are inside fall break

Oct 5 and Oct 12 are fall break — no meeting. We pick back up Oct 19.

docs.text:

That is 12 meetings before winter break. School is out Dec 19 through Jan 10, so there are no meetings on Dec 21, Dec 28, or Jan 4.

docs.title: After the break
docs.text: Kickoff is in January, and the schedule changes completely once build season starts — more days, longer hours. The first Monday back at school is Jan 11, 2027; whether that is a fall-style meeting or the start of build season depends on where kickoff lands.

docs.title: What we do with the time
docs.text:
Two hours a week is not much, so the fall is deliberately ordered:

  • September — toolchain and Java fundamentals. Everyone gets a working deploy before we write anything interesting.
  • October and November — Java through Perscript, then WPILib patterns: subsystems, commands, and the structure DigiLib is built on.
  • December — move to 2027 WPILib as it settles, and start on DigiLib proper.

docs.title: DigiLib
docs.text:
DigiLib is Team 829's own library — the layer between raw WPILib and the robot code we write each season. The point is that a season should not start by rewriting a swerve drive.

This section is being rebuilt

DigiLib 2026 is being reworked for how we want to use it this fall. Nothing on these pages describes last season's code, and nothing here is final until the rework lands. Pages fill in as each piece settles.

docs.title: What is here
docs.text: Page Covers MotorSubsystems Motor-backed mechanisms — the first thing to learn

docs.title: After that
docs.text: Swerve, vision, and the rest come once MotorSubsystems is solid. They are the larger pieces, and they read as variations on the same idea, so there is no point starting there.

docs.title: The 2027 move
docs.text: The 2027 line is a rethink rather than a port: it separates what a mechanism is from what hardware it runs on, so the same mechanism code runs on CTRE hardware, REV hardware, or in simulation. We take that on in December or after kickoff, not before.

docs.title: Getting the code
docs.text: DigiLib lives in the team's private repositories. Ask to be added. Nothing here links to it directly, because the links would 404 for anyone not on the team.

docs.title: MotorSubsystems
docs.text:
Most mechanisms on the robot are a motor turning something — a shooter wheel, an intake roller, an arm, an elevator stage. MotorSubsystems is the part of DigiLib that covers all of them, and it is the first piece to learn. Everything else in the library is a variation on this shape.

Being written as the rework lands

DigiLib 2026 is being modified for our purposes right now. This page gets filled in from the actual code as it settles, rather than from last season's version, so that every signature here matches what is on disk.

docs.title: What this page will cover
docs.text:
• Building one — constructing the hardware and the subsystem, and where that construction lives
  • Configuration — current limits, neutral mode, inversion, and the settings you get wrong once and never again
  • Reading the mechanism — position, velocity, and why these come back as unit types rather than bare doubles
  • Driving it — the command that applies a control request, and the difference between a fixed target and one that changes every loop
  • Default commands — what a mechanism does when nothing else wants it
  • Asking whether it got there — conditions as Triggers, so they compose
  • Simulation — running the mechanism without hardware on the desk

Until then, the Java Bootcamp is the thing to be working on.

docs.title: Java Bootcamp
docs.text:
Everyone starts here — first year or fourth, this is the common starting line. Robot code is Java: not "Java-flavoured blocks", actual Java, with types and objects and a compiler that will tell you exactly what it thinks of your work.

You do not need to be good at it before you touch a robot. You do need to stop being surprised by it.

You will not install anything or open VS Code for any of this. That comes after the bootcamp, and the lab computers are already set up when it does.

docs.title: Start with Perscript
docs.text:
Perscript is where you start. It is straight practice — Java, C++, and Python drills — and drilling is the part that actually moves the needle. Reading about a for loop does nothing. Writing forty of them does.

Open Perscript

Work the Java track. Do it on your own time between meetings; we will not spend Monday afternoons watching each other type basic syntax.

docs.title: What you need to be solid on
docs.text:
Before WPILib will make any sense at all:

  • Types and variables — int, double, boolean, and why the difference between int and double division has ended more robot code than any other bug
  • Conditionals and loops — if/else, for, while
  • Methods — parameters, return values, and why a method that does one thing is worth two that do half each
  • Classes and objects — fields, constructors, this
  • Interfaces and inheritance — this one matters more than usual for us, because it is the shape DigiLib is built out of

docs.title: Then: Java the way FRC uses it
docs.text:
FRC Java has habits that general Java tutorials will not teach you, and they are where new programmers get lost even after they can write a loop:

  • Command-based structure — subsystems, commands, and why almost nothing happens in a plain loop
  • Suppliers and lambdas — () -> something, which is everywhere in modern WPILib and looks like line noise until it suddenly doesn't
  • Units — WPILib has a real units library now, and using it is cheaper than debugging a number that turned out to be in the wrong one

Lessons land here as we go

This section fills in over the fall. The sequence follows the meetings on the Meetings page.

docs.title: Commands you will type constantly
docs.text:
./gradlew build      # compile, and download deps the first time
./gradlew deploy     # push code to the robot
./gradlew simulateJava   # run it without a robot
./gradlew clean      # when you suspect the build is lying to you

docs.title: Quick answers
docs.text:
"My deploy can't find the robot." Check the team number in .wpilib/wpilib_preferences.json — it should be 829. Then check you are on the robot's network, not the school wifi.

"It won't build and the error mentions a Java version." You opened the wrong VS Code. Use the 2026 WPILib VS Code shortcut.

"It built yesterday and not today." ./gradlew clean then build again, on wifi.

"Which WPILib do I install?" 2026.2.1. Not the newest one on the page. The lab computers are already set up; ask before installing on your own machine.
